subject: ENGLISH
title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
objective: Use simple regular verbs for past, present, and future time.
introduction: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb. Explore examples, sort cards, practice, and answer five questions.

vocabulary.definition: The time that has already happened.
The time that is still to come.

activities.instruction: Study the idea and listen to the narration.
activities.content: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.

items.prompt: Which statement best matches “Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow”?

options.text: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.

items.explanation: The correct response is “Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.” because it follows the skill explanation: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.
The correct response is “Yesterday we walked.” because it follows the skill explanation: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.

items.prompt: Which choice does not follow the lesson idea?
items.explanation: The correct response is “Yesterday we will walk.” because it follows the skill explanation: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.

items.prompt: Which sentence is about the future?
items.explanation: The correct response is “We will visit tomorrow.” because it follows the skill explanation: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.

items.prompt: Which example should be used in the final review?
items.explanation: The correct response is “Tomorrow we will walk.” because it follows the skill explanation: Regular past verbs often use -ed; present forms depend on the subject; future can use will plus the base verb.
